Kingdom centred on Old Dongola from the 6th c.; the baqt agreement with Muslim Egypt, followed by Abdallah ibn Abi Sarh's raid on Dongola in 651–2; Northern and Central Nubia later united into one state (GHA II ch.12).

Key events
  • Muslim expedition of 31/651–2 reaches Dongola; fierce Nubian resistance forces a truce
  • Baqt treaty: a non-aggression pact that let al-Makurra keep its independence
  • Faras: more than 120 mural paintings found in 1961–4; Nubian churches were painted from the 8th century
  • Decline under Mamluk pressure: losing internal cohesion, Mukurra faced a Mamluk policy aimed at reducing it to a vassal kingdom
  • Justinian's Melkite mission converts Makuria
  • Arab raid on Dongola and the baqt treaty
  • King Merkurios unites Nubia with its capital at Dongola
  • Bishop Paulos rebuilds Faras Cathedral
  • King Kyriakos marches on Fustat to free the Patriarch
  • Qasr Ibrim scroll: Egypt complains the Nubians are not observing the baqt
  • Prince Georgios's embassy to the Caliph al-Mu'tasim
  • Faras becomes a metropolitan see under the Nubian bishop Kyros
  • Nubians occupy Upper Egypt as far as Akhmim
  • Ayyubid counter-attack: Turan Shah takes Qasr Ibrim
  • Baybars defeats King Dawud and installs Shakanda
  • Dongola royal building converted into a mosque
  • Mamluk expedition restores Karanbas; Kanz al-Dawla retakes power
  • Last written reference to a king of Nubia

Culture

Converted to Melkite (Orthodox) Christianity by Justinian's mission (567–70), then adopted Monophysitism between 660 and 700 (King Merkurios, from 697, is credited with introducing it); government nomenclature modelled on Byzantine bureaucracy; Polish excavations at Old Dongola identified churches and the royal palace (GHA II ch.12).

Economy

Raids did not interrupt the constant trade between Nubia and Muslim Egypt (GHA II ch.12).

    Arab immigrants flowed steadily into northern Nubia; the Banu 'l-Kanz gained a share of land and leadership through intermarriage and matrilineal succession, and a Kanz candidate claimed the throne as the king's sister's son.

Dating note

End date approximate (kingdom fragmented in 14th–15th c.). Merger with Makuria: date disputed. GHA II ch.12 (Michałowski, pp.332–333) gives two versions: Maqrizi has one king, Qalidurut, ruling central and northern Nubia by the mid-7th c.; 'Christian sources seem to prove that the union of Nubia was the work of King Merkurios, who came to the throne in 697.' Derda & Łajtar (2019, p.136 and n.4): 'perhaps around 630'; the earliest indubitable proof of a greater Makuria including Nobadia is the reign of Merkurios (late 7th–early 8th c.); incorporation probably before the Arab raid on Dongola in 652; Godlewski has suggested the end of the 6th c. Welsby 2002 not read on this point.

ملاحظة التأريخ

End date approximate (kingdom fragmented in 14th–15th c.). Merger with Makuria: date disputed. GHA II ch.12 (Michałowski, pp.332–333) gives two versions: Maqrizi has one king, Qalidurut, ruling central and northern Nubia by the mid-7th c.; 'Christian sources seem to prove that the union of Nubia was the work of King Merkurios, who came to the throne in 697.' Derda & Łajtar (2019, p.136 and n.4): 'perhaps around 630'; the earliest indubitable proof of a greater Makuria including Nobadia is the reign of Merkurios (late 7th–early 8th c.); incorporation probably before the Arab raid on Dongola in 652; Godlewski has suggested the end of the 6th c. Welsby 2002 not read on this point. يحتاج تحقق
